title: Customer Portal Solutions: How to Pick the Right Fit for Your Business (May 2026)
summary: Compare customer portal solutions to find the right fit for your business. Security, features, and implementation options explained. May 2026 guide.
body_text: Your support inbox is full of requests that clients could handle themselves if they just had a login: checking order status, downloading past invoices, seeing ticket updates, or grabbing shared files. That's the core problem customer portal solutions are built to solve, but the market is crowded with options that all claim to do the same thing. You're weighing plug-and-play tools, open source builds, specialized software for consultants, and configurable app builders, and the differences aren't always obvious from a pricing page. Small businesses need something fast to set up; larger teams need deep integrations and granular permissions; regulated industries need compliance built in from day one. We're breaking down what makes a working customer portal, how to compare free versus paid tiers, what features matter by business type, and how to match your workflow to the right fit without overbuying on complexity you don't need. TLDR: Customer portal solutions let clients access data, submit requests, and track orders 24/7 without contacting your team. 61% of customers prefer self-service for simple tasks; portals reduce ticket volume and manual follow-up. Look for role-based access, file sharing, ticket tracking, SSO, and integrations with your existing tools. Security requirements vary: healthcare and legal portals must meet SOC 2 or HIPAA compliance requirements from day one. Stacker connects to your spreadsheets or databases and uses AI to generate a working portal in minutes without code. What Is a Customer Portal Solution? A customer portal solution is a secure, web-based space where your clients, customers, or partners can log in to access information, submit requests, track orders, view documents, and manage their relationship with your business without contacting you directly. The core idea is self-service. Rather than routing every question through email or phone, customers get direct access to what they need, when they need it. Most customer portal solutions include a few common building blocks: A login system with role-based access, so each user only sees what's relevant to them A central place to view account data, past orders, invoices, or case history Tools for submitting support tickets, uploading files, or filling out forms Notifications or status updates that keep customers informed without manual follow-up The right solution for your business depends on what your customers actually need to do inside that portal and how much flexibility your team has to set it up and maintain it. Why Businesses Are Adopting Customer Portal Solutions Customer expectations have shifted over the past few years. Clients and customers now expect 24/7 access to their account information, support history, and shared documents, without having to wait for an email reply or a callback from a rep. That shift is driving adoption of self-service portal solutions across industries as businesses look to meet customers where their expectations already are. That shift is pushing businesses toward customer portal solutions at a steady pace. Most customers prefer to handle simple tasks on their own rather than wait for support to respond. When customers can log in and get what they need on their own schedule, ticket volume drops, and satisfaction scores tend to rise. For small businesses especially, the best client portal software replaces scattered email threads and manual status updates with a single, organized space where clients can check order status, download invoices, or submit requests. Core Features Every Customer Portal Solution Should Include A customer portal is only as useful as the features backing it up. Before comparing specific tools or pricing tiers, it helps to know which capabilities actually matter so you can compare options against your real needs, not just a vendor's feature list. Here are the core features worth looking for: Secure login and role-based access control so different users only see what's relevant to them, whether that's a client reviewing their own account or an admin managing the full dataset. A self-service dashboard where customers can check order status, submit requests, or access documents without contacting your team directly. File sharing and document management that lets you exchange contracts, invoices, or reports in one organized place. Ticket or case tracking to keep support requests visible and accountable on both sides. Notifications and messaging to keep customers informed without relying on separate email threads. Integration with your existing tools, such as your CRM, billing system, or help desk, so data stays consistent across your workflow. The right combination depends on your use case. A consulting firm focuses on document exchange and project updates. A SaaS company may weigh ticket tracking and self-service heavily. A small business running client accounts might need only a secure login, a dashboard, and file sharing to start. Security and Compliance Requirements for Customer Portals When customers log in to view invoices, submit support tickets, or access sensitive documents, security stops being optional . A breach in your customer portal can expose client data, damage trust, and trigger regulatory penalties that far outweigh the cost of building things right the first time. Here are the core security requirements to look for in any customer portal solution: Role-based access control lets you restrict what each user sees based on their account, team, or permission level, so a customer never sees another customer's records. SSL encryption and data encryption at rest protect data in transit and at rest. Single sign-on (SSO) support lets customers log in through an identity provider they already trust, reducing password fatigue and credential risk. Audit logs track who accessed or changed what, which is often a requirement for SOC 2, HIPAA, or GDPR compliance. Two-factor authentication (2FA) adds a second verification step, sharply reducing unauthorized access from stolen credentials. If your business handles healthcare data, financial records, or serves enterprise clients, confirm that your chosen solution carries the relevant certifications before committing. Many vendors will list SOC 2 Type II or GDPR compliance on their security pages, but the scope of that coverage varies. Ask directly whether the certification covers the features you plan to use. Measuring the ROI of Customer Portal Solutions Before committing budget to any customer portal solution, you need a clear picture of what success looks like. ROI here goes beyond cost savings — it covers time recovered, support ticket volume, client satisfaction scores, and how quickly your team can onboard new customers. A few metrics worth tracking from day one: Support ticket deflection rate: the percentage of questions resolved through self-service before they reach your team. Client onboarding time: how many days it takes a new customer to become fully active. Portal adoption rate: the share of clients who log in and engage regularly. Staff hours reallocated: time your team gets back from manual status updates and repetitive emails. Set a baseline before you go live, then compare at 30, 60, and 90 days post-deployment to see where the portal is actually moving the needle. Build vs Buy: Comparing Implementation Approaches When choosing a customer portal solution, one of the first decisions you'll face is whether to build something from scratch or buy an existing product. Each path has real trade-offs worth thinking through before you commit. Building a Custom Portal Building gives you full control over features, design, and integrations. For companies with unique workflows or strict data requirements, that flexibility can be worth the investment. The downside is cost and time. Custom development often runs into six figures and takes months before anything is live. Buying an Off-the-Shelf Solution Pre-built software gets you up and running faster, often within days. You trade some flexibility for speed and lower upfront cost. Most tools in this category cover the core needs well: document sharing, ticketing, status tracking, and client logins. A Middle Path: App Builders Tools like Stacker let you build a fully customized portal without writing code. You connect your existing data sources, configure the experience your clients need, and publish without a development team. This suits small businesses and ops teams that need something tailored but can't afford a full build. Customer Portal Solutions for Different Business Types Portal requirements shift significantly based on who logs in and what they need to accomplish. A B2B buyer managing a multi-year contract has very different expectations from a patient accessing health records or a contractor checking their job queue. Business Type Who Logs In Key Needs B2B Buyers, procurement contacts Contract access, order history, multi-user accounts Professional services Consulting or legal clients Document sharing, project updates, and billing Vendor/partner Contractors, suppliers Job assignments, submissions, compliance docs Customer support End users Ticket tracking, knowledge base Healthcare/legal Patients, clients Secure records, case status updates Real estate/agencies Clients, buyers Docs, deliverable approvals, project progress Manufacturing Distributors, buyers Order tracking, inventory visibility B2B and vendor portals typically need the most granular permission controls, since multiple people from the same organization may log in with different access levels. A healthcare or legal portal adds compliance requirements on top of that baseline. Matching Portal Features to Business Context Not every portal needs every feature. A consulting firm running a client portal for document sharing and project updates typically does not need inventory visibility. A manufacturing distributor, on the other hand, may care deeply about real-time order tracking and very little about case status workflows. Starting with your specific user type helps you avoid overbuying features you won't use. Small businesses and solo consultants often favor ease of setup and low cost over deep customization, making lighter-weight solutions a sensible starting point. B2B companies with multiple buyer contacts per account need role-based access that ties permissions to organizations rather than individual users. Compliance-sensitive industries like healthcare and legal require portals that meet data security and compliance standards from the start, not as an afterthought. Common Implementation Challenges and How to Overcome Them Even well-chosen customer portal software can run into friction during rollout. Knowing where teams typically get stuck helps you sidestep the same issues. Here are the most common challenges and practical ways to work through them: User adoption often stalls when the portal adds steps instead of removing them. Keep the interface focused on what clients actually need to do, and walk new users through it before expecting self-service. Data migration from spreadsheets or legacy systems takes longer than expected. Audit your existing records before setup, identify what needs cleaning, and migrate in stages rather than all at once. Permission errors are a frequent early headache. Test role-based access thoroughly with a small group before opening the portal to all clients. Single sign-on and authentication setup can trip up non-technical teams. Choose software that offers pre-built integrations with your existing identity provider to reduce configuration work. Keeping portal content current is an ongoing responsibility, not a one-time task. Assign a clear owner for updates so clients never encounter stale information. How Stacker Helps Businesses Build Custom Portals With AI Stacker takes a different approach to customer portals by letting you build one from your own data using AI. Instead of configuring a rigid off-the-shelf tool, you connect your existing data sources and generate a working app in minutes. Here is what that looks like in practice: You connect a data source such as Airtable, Google Sheets, or a SQL database, and Stacker reads its schema to understand your data structure. AI then generates a portal tailored to your data, which you can refine using a visual editor with no coding required. You control exactly who sees what through role-based permissions, so clients only access their own records. Customers can submit forms, track requests, view documents, and update their own information directly through the portal. This works well for small businesses that need a client-facing portal without hiring a developer, and for ops teams that want to stop routing every request through email. If your data already lives in a spreadsheet or database, Stacker can turn it into a working portal in hours compared to the 3–6 months a custom build typically requires. Final Thoughts on Customer Portal Solutions for Your Business A working customer portal replaces scattered email threads and repetitive status updates with one organized space where clients can help themselves. The setup matters less than whether your customers can log in and get what they need without waiting on your team. Start with secure access, a simple dashboard, and the documents or tracking features your clients ask about most. Book a demo if you want to build something custom from your data without a development team. The right portal should feel like a relief for both sides, not another tool to manage. FAQ What's the best customer portal software for a small business? The best fit depends on your needs: if you want something up and running quickly with minimal setup, tools like Zendesk or HubSpot work well for support-focused portals. If you need a custom portal that connects to your existing spreadsheets or databases without writing code, Stacker lets you build one tailored to your workflow in hours rather than months. Can I build a customer portal without hiring a developer? Yes. Tools like Stacker use AI to generate a working portal from your existing data sources, no coding required. You connect your spreadsheets or databases, describe what your clients need to access, and Stacker builds a secure, branded portal you can refine through conversation. Customer portal solutions vs building a custom portal from scratch? Pre-built solutions get you live faster and cost less upfront, typically launching within days for a few hundred dollars per month. Custom development gives you complete control but usually requires six figures and months of work before anything goes live. App builders like Stacker offer a middle path: fully customized portals built on your data without hiring developers. How long does customer portal implementation typically take? Implementation timelines vary by approach: off-the-shelf tools can go live in days but may require workflow adjustments to fit their structure. AI-powered app builders like Stacker generate working portals in minutes to hours, with refinement taking days to weeks, depending on complexity. Custom development typically spans 3-6 months from requirements gathering to launch. What security features should a customer portal include? Every customer portal needs role-based access control so clients only see their own data, SSL encryption for data in transit, and audit logs to track who accessed what. If you handle regulated data or serve enterprise clients, confirm the solution is SOC 2 Type II- or GDPR-compliant and covers the specific features you plan to use.

title: Origami vs RocketReach: Which Contact Finder Wins for 2026?
summary: Origami vs RocketReach: Prompt-driven AI live search vs static database. Compare free plans, pricing, data freshness, niche coverage, and ease of use in 2026.
body_text: Quick Answer: If you need a prompt-driven AI agent that searches the live web for any ideal customer profile — from local paving contractors to enterprise SaaS buyers — Origami is the stronger pick. Its free plan (1,000 credits, no credit card) and natural‑language interface let you bypass filters and static databases. RocketReach, with 700M+ stored profiles, is a solid choice for quick lookup of known professionals using standard titles, but Origami wins when you want fresh, live‑web data and can describe your ICP in plain English, not with Boolean filters. Side‑by‑side comparison Tool Free Plan (Yes/No) Starting Price Best For Main Limitation Origami Yes Free, then $29/mo Prompt‑driven prospecting, any ICP, live‑web data, local/SMBs. Not a pre‑built static directory; relies on live crawl, so results take a few seconds. RocketReach Yes (0 exports) $69/mo Quick lookup of known contacts by name/email, enterprise sales with common titles. Static database refreshed periodically; less coverage for niche, offline personas. What’s the fundamental difference between the two tools? RocketReach is a searchable directory — it aggregates public profiles from LinkedIn, web sources, and other databases into a massive repository of over 700 million people. You search by name, company, or job title and get back email addresses and phone numbers. The data is refreshed periodically, so some contacts may be months out of date, especially for roles that change frequently (like SDRs, marketing managers, or founders of young companies). Origami is an AI agent that works like a virtual SDR. Instead of filtering through a static database, you type a prompt — for example, “find general managers at family‑owned HVAC companies in Texas that have been in business over 10 years but don’t use any digital marketing.” Origami then crawls the live web (company websites, news articles, social media, government directories, etc.), identifies relevant people, and enriches them with verified email addresses and phone numbers — all in one flow. There’s no pre‑wired database; it’s real‑time discovery. This architectural difference matters a lot when your ideal customer profile doesn’t fit a standard corporate ladder. If you sell to local service businesses, regional distributors, niche manufacturers, or any segment where decision‑makers don’t always have polished LinkedIn profiles, a static database will have significant gaps. Origami was built to fill those gaps. How fresh is the data — live web search vs a stored database? RocketReach refreshes its database on a periodic schedule; the exact frequency isn’t publicly documented, but the data is not real‑time. A contact who changed jobs three months ago might still appear under their old title until the next refresh cycle. For many enterprise sales use cases, that’s acceptable. Origami’s live‑web crawl means every search in 2026 pulls the most current public information available at that moment. If a company just posted a job opening for a new VP of Operations, Origami can find that signal and include it in the results. This is especially powerful for: Fast‑growing startups where roles change every quarter. Local services (roofers, electricians, plumbers) whose digital footprint might only be on a state licensing board website. Niche verticals (agricultural equipment, medical aesthetics, trade schools) where standard databases lack up‑to‑date coverage. You don’t have to worry about “stale data” because you’re not querying a snapshot — you’re querying the internet. Which tool actually finds more contacts for weird, non‑standard ICPs? This is where the architectural choice becomes clear. RocketReach is built for volume — it has hundreds of millions of profiles. But those profiles overwhelmingly come from platforms like LinkedIn, which means they skew toward white‑collar, corporate, and tech‑savvy professionals. For a typical B2B SaaS company selling to chief revenue officers, it works reasonably well. If your ICP is, say, the owner of a family‑owned paving company, an athletic director at a rural school district, or a geriatric care manager with no LinkedIn presence, RocketReach (like most contact databases) hits a wall. Those people simply aren’t in the database. Origami was designed for exactly these “offline” buyers. By searching the live web — including government directories, membership sites, news articles, and even PDFs — it can surface contacts that static databases cannot. One Origami user described spending “hours upon hours” manually scraping Google Maps for paving contractors; with Origami, the same work took “about five minutes.” That’s the power of a prompt‑driven web crawler. Ease of use: can you really get a list in five minutes without filters? Yes. RocketReach requires you to use filters: job title, company name, location, industry, and sometimes more. If you know exactly who you’re looking for, that’s fine, but if your ICP doesn’t map neatly to a “job title” box, you’ll spend time guessing and iterating. Origami lets you describe your ICP in natural language. You type something like: “Find the operations managers at independently owned craft breweries in Colorado that self‑distribute and have fewer than 50 employees.” The AI agent then researches, filters, and enriches — no click‑heavy UI, no Boolean logic. Teams that previously spent half a day building a list in Apollo or RocketReach report getting workable results in under ten minutes with Origami. The interface is literally a chat; you can refine it conversationally (“remove any that are franchise locations”). That’s why teams without dedicated RevOps or sales engineers particularly love it. Pricing: how much do Origami and RocketReach really cost? Origami’s pricing is built for teams that want to start small and scale. The free plan includes 1,000 credits with no credit card required. Paid plans start at $29/month for 2,000 credits, scaling up to a Pro plan at $129/month (9,000 credits) and an Enterprise tier with custom credits. Credits are used for search queries and enrichments, so you only pay for the leads you actually need — not for a huge database you barely touch. RocketReach offers a free plan with zero exports (you can look up a few profiles but can’t download data). Paid plans begin at $69/month (billed monthly) or $399/year for 1,200 exports per year. The next tier is $119/month for 6,000 exports, and the Ultimate plan is $209/month for 20,000 exports. Note that “exports” are individual contact records; if you need to pull a large list every month, costs can climb quickly. For a solo founder or a small team doing a few hundred prospects per month, Origami’s free plan or $29/month entry point is dramatically cheaper. Even at the $129/month Pro level, you often get more targeted, higher‑intent leads than you would by churning through a generic database. When is RocketReach still the better choice? We’re not here to bash RocketReach — it’s a useful tool that millions of salespeople rely on. RocketReach excels in a few specific scenarios: You need to look up a known person. If you already have a name and company, and just want the direct email and phone number, RocketReach’s lookup is fast and convenient. Your ICP is standard corporate roles. Selling to VPs of Sales at Fortune 1000 companies? The database will have deep coverage because those profiles are well‑represented on LinkedIn and in public data. You want a large contact database to manually browse. Some salespeople prefer to explore by company, dig through employee lists, and cherry‑pick leads. RocketReach’s directory approach supports that “browsing” behavior better than Origami’s prompt‑based search. You’re heavily invested in the RocketReach ecosystem. If your team already uses RocketReach’s Chrome extension, API, and CRM integrations, switching might not be worth the migration effort. If your primary need is intent‑driven prospecting where you don’t know the exact names ahead of time, or your ICP is niche, local, or hard‑to‑find, Origami is the smarter investment. Which tool should you pick for your team size and ICP? Solo founders and lean teams: Origami’s free plan and simple chat interface make it a no‑brainer. You can validate your ICP and build a list in minutes without learning a complex platform. Mid‑market companies with a specific vertical focus: If you sell to commercial roofing, medical spas, third‑party logistics providers, or any segment where the best contacts aren’t on LinkedIn, Origami’s live‑web search will uncover leads that RocketReach simply doesn’t have. Large enterprise sales teams selling to other large enterprises: Both tools work, but if you have a RevOps team that can set up detailed filters and your ICP is “VP of Finance at companies with 1,000+ employees,” RocketReach may be sufficient. However, even then, Origami adds value by finding trigger events (e.g., a recent funding round or a new executive hire) that static databases miss. Agencies and lead‑gen services: If you need to deliver hundreds of thousands of contacts per month to clients, RocketReach’s export‑oriented model may be more cost‑effective at that volume, provided your clients’ target audiences are well‑represented in the database. Origami is better for quality over quantity, where each lead is researched and enriched in real time. The verdict Choose Origami if you value live‑web data freshness, struggle to find contacts in niche or local markets, or want the fastest possible list building without complex filters. The free plan lets you test with zero risk, and the conversational AI agent dramatically reduces the time your team spends on prospecting. For modern GTM teams that can describe their ICP in plain English, Origami is the more flexible, future‑proof option in 2026. Choose RocketReach if your sales motion relies on quickly looking up email addresses and phone numbers for known contacts at large, well‑known companies, or if you need a massive, browsable contact directory. It’s a proven workhorse for enterprise sales teams with predictable, standard ICPs. If you’re still on the fence, try both — but start with Origami’s free plan. You’ll have a refreshed, ready‑to‑use prospect list before you’ve finished configuring RocketReach’s filters.

title: Made in Salzbergen: Why Germany’s Wind Future Depends on Reliable Execution
summary: The conditions for building new wind projects in Germany are evolving rapidly. Developers are working within a sophisticated landscape of auction tariffs and evolving regulations. Planning reforms have helped bring more permits into the industry, but auction volumes have not always kept pace. This environment rewards precision and high-level coordination. The result is a business model that prioritizes disciplined execution and operational certainty.
body_text: The conditions for building new wind projects in Germany are evolving rapidly. Developers are working within a sophisticated landscape of auction tariffs and evolving regulations. Planning reforms have helped bring more permits into the industry, but auction volumes have not always kept pace . This environment rewards precision and high-level coordination. The result is a business model that prioritizes disciplined execution and operational certainty. Despite this, ambition is not in short supply in the country’s wind industry. Germany remains one of Europe’s most important renewable hubs for onshore wind, with a deep industrial base and a long history of community participation in the energy transition. Wind turbines still need to remain cost-competitive, but they also need to help customers improve project financial models through manufacturing, transport, installation, and long-term operation. For Dimitri Schneider, managing director and executive sourcing leader at GE Vernova, the answer begins with “reliability at scale” as a competitive advantage in today’s wind industry — delivering proven solutions through disciplined execution and continuous improvement. The company’s 6.5 MW-164m onshore wind turbine is the latest evolution of an established turbine family, with processes from factory to site already tested and standardized. Reliable Performance over Time The 6.5 MW-164m is produced at GE Vernova’s Salzbergen manufacturing site in northwestern Germany, where the focus on repeatability recently reached a new landmark. The facility has now produced more than 25 GW of onshore wind turbine capacity, demonstrating a disciplined product strategy and a model of partnership in one of Europe’s most competitive regions for wind energy. The hub line at GE Vernova's Salzbergen wind facility. GE Vernova’s 6.5 MW-164m turbine is both a driver and a product of this success. Launched globally in 2019, the machine builds on years of operating experience and project data. “Quality, long-term performance, and long-term reliability have been at the forefront of our product development,” explains Marcas Breatnach, Northern Europe sales leader for Onshore Wind at GE Vernova. “You can only achieve a low levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) if the turbine performs well over the full duration of its use.” This shift elevates the importance of consistent execution. Today, developers benefit from a closer alignment between the project plan and the actual work. Auction prices have made operational excellence more important than ever. Consistent performance over the operating life of the asset has a direct commercial impact, which means LCOE not only is driven by turbine rating or cost but also depends on proven reliability. Community Impact The milestone has a distinctly German character, with the turbines marking Salzbergen’s 25th gigawatt of production bound for a community-owned wind farm — part of a segment that has long defined the country’s renewable energy story. In Germany, local communities aren’t just hosts for new infrastructure; they participate directly in the transition, with a clear stake in how cleaner power is developed, financed, and delivered. This reinforces the significance of the milestone, Breatnach says, and reflects GE Vernova’s goal to work pragmatically with partners of different sizes, from large utilities and developers to neighborhood projects. “Our commitment is to pragmatism and partnering with customers on an equal footing, whatever their scale.” Local production at Salzbergen creates local jobs ( the site employs around 700 people ) and strengthens and shortens the German supply chain, while also giving developers and operators confidence that critical energy infrastructure is being produced close to end users. The Road Ahead As a key node in GE Vernova’s wider European wind operations, Salzbergen’s reach extends well beyond Germany. The site is “positioned with strong logistics infrastructure,” says Schneider. It also exports internationally, connecting German industrial capability to renewable projects across the continent. Its central location allows the company to work closely with suppliers, improving coordination and responsiveness when conditions change. In a sector marked by supply chain disruption, regulatory pressure, and the need to speed up construction, this is vital. Looking ahead, Schneider believes three factors will determine the success of Europe’s decarbonization effort: the ability to deliver, resilience, and collaboration. Ambitious targets will translate into new capacity as the industry completes projects with precision, with technologies that perform under real-world conditions and relationships that hold over time. “At GE Vernova, we believe Salzbergen represents exactly this mindset,” Schneider says, “combining reliability, partnership, and industry strength to help scale onshore wind energy across Europe and beyond.”

title: Your hotel network infrastructure is about business, not tech
summary: Hotel network infrastructure built on quick fixes creates technical debt. Learn how to reduce downtime and align your network with hotel business goals.
body_text: When something breaks or isn’t working right, the instinct for most hotel operators is to move quickly to take care of the problem. In most cases, that means scrambling to find a single product that will resolve the issue (at least temporarily). Guests complaining about poor Wi‑Fi connectivity ? Add more access points. Cameras at the edge don’t have power? Drop in a small switch or PoE injector. Meeting rooms with legacy copper or coax? Pull new cable. But taking a shortcut now—or not verifying existing hotel network infrastructure before adding something new—means paying for it later. While every purchase is meant to address a specific challenge, it also adds another vendor, another trade and another schedule to coordinate. This makes the network more complicated to build, maintain and scale . And no one is thinking about or accountable for the big picture or long-term vision. The hidden cost of solving problems one device at a time To guests, these individual upgrades may make the property feel modern. Behind the scenes, however, your team is responding to complaints, working around operational bottlenecks and managing tech projects that never catch up. And it’s all because problems are being treated as isolated issues instead of signs that the hotel network infrastructure needs attention. This pattern turns into technical debt . And it accumulates when quick fixes are the default. If you’re taking care of today’s problem with a local workaround, then every future change will be harder and more expensive because you have to deal with all the shortcuts and patches that came before.

title: Beyond the Buzzwords: Intelligent DDoS Defense for Modern CISOs
summary: FatPipe not only reduces malicious traffic, but ensures that the mitigation doesn’t disrupt the users and services it is meant to protect.
body_text: If you are treating DDoS mitigation as the last item on your checklist, it may be time to think again. It belongs in the same conversation as WAN resilience, failover, business continuity, and service availability. Picture the CISO at your organization, quietly scrolling through the latest cybersecurity headlines before the office wakes up. Their newsfeed is full of jargon: volumetric attacks, protocol exploits, application-layer strikes, hit-and-run incursions, and multi-vector attacks. It is a confusing lexicon, but the real threat is more subtle. While the CISO may rely on frameworks and best practices, cyber attackers are working from a different playbook. Their tactics are unpredictable: blending attack types, shifting strategies, and overwhelming networks with traffic spikes or coordinated connection floods. The result is that security appliances, servers, and online services can collapse under pressure, no matter how prepared you thought you were. This is where intelligent inbound control comes into play. A blind DDoS block may drop all incoming traffic to an attacked subnet, such as through null routing or broad upstream blocking. While this can stop attack traffic, it can also make the protected service unreachable for legitimate users. FatPipe’s approach through inbound PRR is more selective. Instead of applying a one-size-fits-all response to inbound traffic, FatPipe enables a more intelligent, policy-driven approach. By attaching DDoS protection to an inbound PRR policy, traffic can be evaluated with greater context, including protocol, service, port, source, destination, and session behavior. This makes mitigation more precise, controlled, and aligned with legitimate business traffic needs. EV3 augments this approach with real-time monitoring and session rate control. Rate Limiting with Trusted Network Awareness Trusted networks should be treated differently. Instead of applying the same harsh response to every inbound request, policies can be designed so that known or trusted networks receive appropriate priority, while unknown or excessive traffic is rate-limited. In this way, FatPipe helps maintain service availability during abnormal traffic conditions without unnecessarily cutting off valid users. FatPipe’s DDoS protection is not a blind “ block everything ” approach. It is a controlled mitigation method that uses inbound PRR, intelligent tracking, trusted-network-aware policy design, and real-time session monitoring to limit excessive traffic while preserving legitimate access wherever possible. Small businesses need simple, affordable continuity. Large enterprises need scalable, layered resilience. FatPipe’s solution was conceived to address the common problem behind both: keeping legitimate business traffic online even when part of the network is under stress or attack. That significance becomes clear during an active attack. The objective is not only to reduce malicious traffic, but also to make sure the mitigation response does not disrupt the very users and services it is meant to protect. Please Like and Share

title: Marking a Pivotal Step in Transformation Journey, Carrier Integrates its EcoEnergy Insights™ and Abound™ Digital Solutions | News
summary: EcoEnergy Insights now goes to market as Carrier Abound | News
body_text: PALM BEACH GARDENS, Fla., Oct 7, 2024 - Carrier Global Corporation (NYSE: CARR), global leader in intelligent climate and energy solutions, announced today that its EcoEnergy Insights™ business will now go to market globally as Carrier Abound™. EcoEnergy Insights, a leading provider of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Internet of Things (IoT) solutions for building and equipment operations will also re-badge its CORTIX™ suite of solutions as Abound solutions. With these changes, Carrier will now offer its customers a comprehensive and cohesive suite of digital solutions and digitally enabled services to achieve outcomes in sustainability, health and well-being, and asset management. "This integration marks a pivotal step in Carrier's transformation journey to become a global leader in intelligent climate and energy solutions," said Mead Rusert, Vice President, Building Technologies, Carrier. "Bringing our solutions and expertise into one group accelerates our efforts and enhances customer service − further demonstrating our commitment to developing solutions for sustainable building operations." For nearly 15 years, EcoEnergy Insights has been recognized for its award-winning solutions that have helped customers save over 6 billion kWh globally.1 This energy savings is equivalent to the greenhouse gas emissions produced by nearly one million gasoline-powered passenger vehicles driven for an entire year.2 Leveraging Carrier's expertise in energy-efficient HVAC systems, Carrier Abound aims to enhance operational efficiencies, drive customer engagement and enable smarter, more sustainable building management. The solutions are designed to create value through a combination of innovative technology, advanced analytics and advisory services, ultimately helping customers achieve their sustainability goals. 1Calculated to the International Performance Measurement and Verification Protocol, 2011 through 2024. 2Equivalency calculation per U.S. EPA Greenhouse Gas Equivalencies Calculator. About Carrier Carrier Global Corporation, global leader in intelligent climate and energy solutions, is committed to creating solutions that matter for people and our planet for generations to come. From the beginning, we've led in inventing new technologies and entirely new industries. Today, we continue to lead because we have a world-class, diverse workforce that puts the customer at the center of everything we do. For more information, visit corporate.carrier.com or follow Carrier on social media at @Carrier .
